en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Marks Adorned with a Hundredfold Merits, translated once more by the Tripitaka Master Divākara of India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying in the city of Śrāvastī at the Universal Wondrous Palace.

World-Honored One, desiring to transform and guide immeasurable sentient beings, you sit upon a lion throne adorned with jewels, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and an incalculable multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. All of them pay their respects, surrounding you on every side, gazing up at the World-Honored One with body and mind unmoving.

At that time, there was a great bodhisattva in that assembly named Mañjuśrī. Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
I have heard that the Tathāgata possesses a great mass of merit. What is the measure of this great mass of merit?
I pray that the World-Honored One will explain it for me, so as to benefit immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings and cause their aspirations to be fully satisfied.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:

"Good son! You have already transcended all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; you are able, with a mind of wisdom and great compassion, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a meaning for the sake of all sentient beings. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you."

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings in a single Jambudvīpa were to possess the mass of merit from practicing the ten virtuous actions; if that mass of merit were calculated, measured, and multiplied until it reached a full hundredfold, it would constitute the mass of merit of a single universal monarch (cakravartin) ruling over the four continents with sovereign power, endowed with the seven treasures and possessed of a thousand sons.”

What are the seven treasures? First is the golden wheel treasure; second is the white elephant treasure; third is the deep-blue horse treasure; fourth is the divine jewel treasure; fifth is the jade woman treasure; sixth is the treasurer treasure; and seventh is the military commander treasure.
His thousand sons are each majestic, handsome, brave, and strong, capable of defeating enemies.
Mañjuśrī! This is called the mass of merit belonging to a wheel-turning sage king.

“Mañjuśrī! If one were to calculate and measure the mass of merit possessed by such a wheel-turning sage king and all sentient beings throughout the four continents, and if that mass of merit were multiplied a hundredfold, it would constitute the mass of merit of Śakra, the lord of the gods in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.”

“Mañjuśrī! If the entire mass of merit belonging to the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and all sentient beings in the four continents were calculated and measured, and that mass of merit were increased a hundredfold, it would constitute the mass of merit of a Māra who governs, protects, and maintains the sixth heaven of the desire realm.”

“Mañjuśrī! Thus, the mass of merit belonging to this sixth sovereign Māra of the devas, as well as the entire mass of merit possessed by all sentient beings in the four continents—when these masses of merit are calculated, weighed, and multiplied a full hundred thousand times, they constitute the mass of merit of a single Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna who, with a mind of loving-kindness, illuminates and observes a small chiliocosm.”

“Mañjuśrī! In this way, the mass of merit possessed by the Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna who illuminates and observes a small thousand-world system, as well as the mass of merit possessed by all sentient beings in that world—when this mass of merit is calculated, reckoned, and multiplied again by a hundred thousand times, it constitutes the mass of merit possessed by the Brahmā King of the Second Dhyāna of a medium thousand-world system.”

“Mañjuśrī! If one were to take the mass of merit possessed by the Brahmā kings of the second dhyāna in such a medium chiliocosm, as well as all sentient beings in those worlds, and calculate and weigh that mass of merit again multiplied by a hundred thousand times, it would equal the mass of merit of Maheśvara within the fourth dhyāna who observes with a heart of loving-kindness throughout a great trichiliocosm.”
“Mañjuśrī! This Mahesvara, lord of the great trichiliocosm, is not accomplished by means of meager roots of goodness. Why is this?

Because Maheśvara possesses great wisdom and great majestic power, when the world-receptacle is about to be re-established after being consumed by the fires of destruction, he sends down a great rain from the fourth dhyāna heaven that falls continuously and without interruption for five intermediate kalpas. This water pervades the entire great trichiliocosm and rises as far as the Brahma-world; such drops of rain, falling without deficiency or diminution, are all fully known by Maheśvara, the lord of that great trichiliocosm.
“Mañjuśrī! Such a mass of merit as belongs to Maheśvara—such a mass of merit is called ‘Brahma-merit. Mañjuśrī!”

If one were to calculate and measure the mass of merit possessed by Maheśvara, the lord of this trichiliocosm, as well as all sentient beings in that world, and then multiply that mass of merit by immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of times, it would constitute the mass of merit of a single, preeminent Pratyekabuddha.
“Mañjuśrī! Let alone this single great trichiliocosm.

Suppose all the masses of merit possessed by all sentient beings and pratyekabuddhas throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions were combined; if such a mass of merit were calculated and measured until it reached an immeasurable hundred-thousand-ten-million-fold increase, it would constitute the mass of merit of a bodhisattva in his final birth.”

“Mañjuśrī! If one were to calculate and compare the mass of merit of a bodhisattva in their final birth with the mass of merit possessed by all sentient beings throughout all worlds as far as the limits of space in the ten directions—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; whether possessing form or formless; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—the mass of merit of those sentient beings, when multiplied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of times, constitutes the mass of merit contained within a single pore of that Tathāgata’s body.”
Mañjuśrī! In this way, the Tathāgata’s body has ninety-nine thousand pores, and each of these pores possesses the immeasurable mass of merit as described above.

“Mañjuśrī! Thus, the mass of merit contained within all the pores of a Tathāgata—if one were to calculate and measure such a mass of merit and multiply it by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions, it would constitute the mass of merit for a single secondary mark among the marks of excellence on the body of a Tathāgata.”
“Mañjuśrī! Thus, the secondary marks of the Tathāgata’s body, briefly stated in number, are eighty kinds.
What are these eighty?
First, the crown of the head is perfectly full; second, the hairline is beautifully adorned; third, the color of the hair is deep blue-black;
fourth, the hair is fragrant and sweet-smelling; fifth, the hair is exceedingly soft; sixth, the hair is not disheveled;
seventh, the hair is neither too sparse nor too thick; eighth, the hair grows constantly; ninth, the roots of the hair...
10. The hair curls at the tips; 11. the hair is shaped like a flower garland; 12. the hair is in the form of the letter *śrī*;
13. the face is level and symmetrical; 14. the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft is fully developed; 15.
the color of the eyebrows is deep blue-black; 16. the eyebrows are not disheveled; 17.
17. His two eyes are beautiful; 18. His two eyes are long and wide; 19. His two eyes are pure; 20.
His two eyes are bright and clear; 21. The color of his eyes is deep blue and radiant like a blue lotus flower;
22. His ears are very long and well-formed; 23. His ears are without deficiency.
24. His ears are free from blemish; 25. His nose is long, high, and straight;
26. His two cheeks are full; 27. His cheeks are without deficiency;
28. His cheeks are free from blemish; 29. His teeth are perfectly round and even; 30. As for his teeth...
31. His lips are of a beautiful crimson hue, like the *bimba* fruit;
32. His tongue is crimson and soft; 33. His voice is like the roll of thunder; 34. His speech is clear and penetrating; 35.
His body is perfectly proportioned and complete; 36. The flesh of his body is full and well-formed.
37. The flesh of the body is level and even; 38. the flesh of the body is soft and supple;
39. the body is gradually straight and upright; 40. the parts of the body are proportionate; 41.
the body is exceedingly well-rounded and beautiful; 42. the body is without deficiency or diminution; 43. his body...
Forty-fourth, his body is supple; forty-fifth, his body is pure and clean; forty-sixth, his body is light and subtle;
forty-seventh, his body is immovable; forty-eighth, his body is exceedingly dignified and majestic;
forty-ninth, his body is free from blemish or impurity; fiftieth, the radiance of his body dispels darkness.
51. His abdomen is beautiful; 52. His abdomen is full and rounded; 53. His abdomen is not protruding; 54.
His navel is deep and well-concealed; 55. His navel is not crooked; 56.
His navel is situated in its proper place; 57. The area beneath his armpits is flat and full.
Seventeenth: his arms and elbows are slender and long; fifty-eighth: his fingers are full and rounded; fifty-ninth:
his fingers are slender and beautiful; sixtieth: the lines on his palms are deep and auspicious; sixty-first:
the lines on his palms extend straight through; sixty-second: the lines on his palms are not disordered; sixty-third: the lines on his palms are smooth and lustrous.
64. His writing is neither coarse nor fine; 65. His writing is elegant, slender, and sharp;
66. His kneecaps are round and broad; 67. His heels are high and full;
68. His feet tread the ground well; 69. He walks turning to the right; 70. His gait is like...
Seventy-first, his gait is like that of a bull king; seventy-second, his gait is like that of a swan king;
seventy-third, his stride is majestic and powerful like that of a lion king;
seventy-fourth, the tips of his nails on the hands and feet are all slightly raised; seventy-fifth, the nails of his hands and feet are the color of red copper.
Seventy-sixth, the nails of his hands and feet are all glossy and lustrous; seventy-seventh, his sinews and veins do not protrude;
seventy-eighth, his limbs and joints are dense and firm; seventy-ninth, his sense faculties are free from defilement;
eightieth, those who see him are filled with joy.
Mañjuśrī! As previously explained, these eighty kinds are called the mass of merit of the Tathāgata’s secondary marks. Mañjuśrī!

If one were to calculate and measure the mass of merit contained in the Tathāgata’s eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), and then multiply that mass by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions, it would constitute the mass of merit for a single auspicious mark (*lakṣaṇa*) upon the Tathāgata’s body, such as those on his hands and feet.
Mañjuśrī! Thus, within the hands, feet, and other parts of the Tathāgata, there are eighty kinds of marks on the lines of the webbed fingers and toes.
What are these eighty?
First, the image of Brahmā; second, the image of Śakra; third, the image of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
fourth, the image of Virūḍhaka; fifth, the image of Virūpākṣa; sixth, the image of Vaiśravaṇa;
seventh, the image of the goddess Śrī; eighth, the image of the Sun Devaputra; ninth, [the image of]...
10. An image of the Moon Deva; 11. an image of Varuṇa (Water Deva); 12. an image of Agni (Fire Deva);
13. an image of Vāyu (Wind Deva); 14. an image of Megha (Cloud Deva); 15. an image of the Great Sage (Maharṣi); 16.
an image of the Mountain King (Parvatarāja); 17. an image of a young boy; 18. an image of a young girl.
Eighteenth, the image of a jeweled banner; nineteenth, the image of a parasol; twentieth, the image of a jeweled crown;
twenty-first, the image of a flower garland; twenty-second, the image of a pearl necklace;
twenty-third, the image of an earring; twenty-fourth, the image of an arm seal; twenty-fifth, the image of a jeweled bracelet.
26. Image of a finger-ring; 27. Image of a precious mirror; 28.
Image of a white fly-whisk; 29. Image of the syllable *bhadra*;
30. Image of a flower vase; 31. Image of a *maṇi* jewel; 32. Image of a precious sword; 33. [Image of]...
34. The image of a vajra; 35. the image of a bow; 36. the image of an arrow; 37. the image of a spear; 38. the image of a halberd;
39. the image of an axe; 40. the image of a noose; 41. the image of a long hook.
Forty-first, the image of a chariot-fender; forty-second, the image of a golden mallet;
forty-third, the image of a celestial club; forty-fourth, the image of a celestial drum;
forty-fifth, the image of a celestial conch; forty-sixth, the image of a waist-drum; forty-seventh, the image of a flower garland; forty-eighth, the image of—
50. The image of the palace; 51. the image of the jeweled throne; 52. the image of the bathing pool;
53. the image of the lotus flower; 54. the image of the fine rice; 55. the image of the wheat; 56.
the image of the medicinal herbs; 57. the image of the sacred kusha grass.
56. the image of a flowering tree; 57. the image of a fruit-bearing tree;
58. the image of a garuḍa; 59. the image of a kalaviṅka; 60. the image of a jīvañjīvaka;
61. the image of a peacock; 62. the image of a dove or pigeon; 63. [the image of a]... 60. [repeated].
63) the image of a king of geese; 64) the image of a blue jay; 65) the image of a parrot;
66) the image of a green pheasant; 67) the image of a lion within a wheel;
68) the image of a white elephant from the Snowy Mountains; 69) the image of a nāga king; 70) [the image of a...].
Seventy-first, the form of an elephant king; seventy-second, the form of a horse king;
seventy-third, the form of a deer king; seventy-fourth, the form of an ox king; seventy-fifth, the form of a wild buffalo; seventy-sixth, the form of a cow;
seventy-seventh, the form of a black sheep; seventy-eighth, the form of a giant turtle.
78. The image of the Great Tortoise; 79. The image of the Fish King; 80.
The image of the Conch King. Mañjuśrī!
These eighty kinds thus described are called the mass of merit of the Tathāgata’s secondary marks. "Mañjuśrī!

If one were to calculate and measure the entire mass of merit of these eighty secondary marks of the Tathāgata, and then multiply that mass of merit by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions, it would constitute the mass of merit for a single one of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the body of a Tathāgata."
Mañjuśrī! Such are the marks of a great man of the Tathāgata, numbering thirty-two in all.
What are these thirty-two marks of a great man?
First, his crown is adorned with a fleshy protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), which is perfectly rounded, lofty, and sublime; second, his hair is deep blue-black in color, with each strand curling to the right;
third, his forehead is broad, level, and majestic; fourth, the tuft of hair between his eyebrows (ūrṇā-kośa) is whiter than white jade or snow;
fifth, his eyelashes are as fine and dark as those of a bull king; sixth, his mouth has forty [teeth].
Seventh, his teeth neither increase nor decrease in number; eighth, his teeth are even and closely set without gaps or missing ones;
ninth, his teeth are white and pure without any stains or blackness; tenth, his four canine teeth are exceptionally bright and clean;
eleventh, his jaw is full and rounded like that of a lion king; twelfth, his tongue is supple, thin, broad, and crimson.
12. Among all tastes, he obtains the supreme taste; 13. His speech is like a thunderclap, possessing the Brahma-voice;
14. The collarbone is not visible, as that area is flat and full;
15. Both shoulders are perfectly rounded and without deficiency; 16. When his two arms are extended downward, his hands reach and touch his knees.
Seventeenth, his upper body is like that of a lion king; eighteenth, all the hairs on his body point upward;
nineteenth, his physical form is perfectly proportioned like a nyagrodha tree;
twentieth, his body is sublime and measures seven cubits in height; twenty-first, the skin of his body is entirely...
Twenty-second, his body is golden in color; twenty-third, a single hair grows from each pore;
twenty-fourth, his sexual organ is retracted and concealed, remaining hidden and not manifest; twenty-fifth, his two thighs are round and symmetrical, with well-filled flesh;
twenty-sixth, his calves are well-proportioned and beautiful like those of the king of the eneya deer. Twenty-sixth.
Twenty-sixth, both feet are full and fleshy, without any deficiency; twenty-seventh, the undersides of both soles are entirely flat and full;
twenty-eighth, the skin, flesh, and bones of the feet are all well-developed and prominent;
twenty-ninth, both hands and both feet are entirely soft and supple; thirtieth, both hands and both feet are possessed of webbed membranes.
31. Both his hands and feet are slender and long; 32. Both his hands and feet possess the mark of the wheel. Mañjuśrī!
These thirty-two marks of a great man as thus described are called the Tathāgata’s true marks and his accumulation of merit. “Mañjuśrī!

This accumulation of merit of the thirty-two marks of a great man of the Tathāgata—when this accumulation of merit is calculated and measured, and increased by immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, incalculable, and inconceivable multiples—only then does it form the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-circle conch, the accumulation of merit for the voice that teaches and transforms all sentient beings according to their kinds.”

“Mañjuśrī! In this way, the great Dharma conch of the Tathāgata can, according to the various inclinations of all sentient beings in immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya, and infinite worlds, completely satisfy them according to those inclinations; it preaches the Dharma and transforms them through sounds corresponding to their respective types, thereby benefiting, bringing peace, and happiness to such sentient beings.”

“Mañjuśrī! Just as the voice of that Tathāgata possesses such immeasurable power, so too does the majestic radiance of the Tathāgata; equal to that voice, it likewise possesses such immeasurable power.”

“Mañjuśrī! Just as that Tathāgata possesses such majestic radiance and can exercise such immeasurable power, so too is the body of the Tathāgata; it is equal to that majestic radiance and can likewise exercise such immeasurable power.”
“Mañjuśrī! As has been described above, such a mass of merit is inconceivable and incalculable; it is not something that can be attained by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others.”

Why is this? Because such an accumulation of merit arises from great wisdom and great compassion, and is produced by the all-pervading power of the most supreme vows; therefore, it cannot be attained by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.

“Mañjuśrī! Such a body of wondrous form as that of the Tathāgata is entirely established by all the most supreme purities of giving, precept-keeping, and cultivation, as well as by two causes and conditions.”
What are these two? First, the Tathāgata’s most supreme power of aspiration; second, the Tathāgata’s skillfulness in transforming and guiding beings.
What is meant by the Tathāgata’s skillfulness in transforming and guiding beings?

That is to say, it causes those sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them; it causes those who have already planted roots of goodness to bring them to maturity; and it causes those who have already matured to attain liberation.
By the power of these two kinds of causes and conditions, one thus obtains a body of sublime form. Mañjuśrī!
In this way, the Tathāgata’s body of sublime form is accomplished through two causes and conditions.
The voice of the Tathāgata is also like this, being accomplished through two causes and conditions. "Mañjuśrī!
Thus, all the voices of the Tathāgata are accomplished by means of these two causes and conditions."
The majestic radiance of the Tathāgata is likewise achieved through two causes and conditions.
"Mañjuśrī! Thus, all the majestic radiance of the Tathāgata is accomplished by means of these two causes and conditions."
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is also like this, being accomplished through two causes and conditions. "Mañjuśrī!
Thus, all the teachings of the Tathāgata are accomplished by means of these two causes and conditions."
The practice of the Tathāgata is also like this, being accomplished through two causes and conditions. "Mañjuśrī!

The Tathāgata appears in the world out of a desire to have compassion for all sentient beings; he appears in the world out of a desire to benefit all sentient beings; he appears in the world out of a desire to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings. Because the various natures, inclinations, and aspirations of sentient beings differ from one another, the Tathāgata manifests various bodies endowed with the marks and signs according to their respective dispositions, preaching the Dharma and teaching them to subdue them, leading them into the Buddha-dharma so that they may achieve accomplishment."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, having heard from the Buddha the aforementioned accumulation of merit which benefits all devas and people of the world, spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."

Today I have attained great and wholesome benefit; today I have attained the most supreme state; today I have attained that which is unequaled; today I have attained great auspiciousness. I contemplate the Tathāgata as the great refuge for all sentient beings within the world—one who is pure and immovable like space, difficult to encounter and difficult to meet, whom I have now beheld.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, those bhikṣus and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, filled with joy, joined their palms in reverence, and faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Physical Marks Adorned with a Hundred Merits
